title: Prologue (lines 1–155)
focus: a king who promises to find the truth

teacherSummary.text: Thebes is dying of a plague. Suppliants and a Priest beg King Oedipus, who once saved the city from the Sphinx, to save it again. Creon returns from Delphi: Apollo says the city must drive out the killer of the former king, Laius. Oedipus vows to "make dark things clear" and calls the people together.

context.history: There is no outside record of the first performance; the Standard Ebooks edition dates it to about 429 B.C.E. (Sophocles, ca. 429 B.C.E./2025). Jebb reports the modern theory that the plague of Thebes reflects the Athenian plague of 430 B.C.E. and sets it aside (Jebb, 1893/1902, Introduction, § 15). Storr's line numbers are English lines, not Greek.

significance: The man who solves riddles sets out to solve one more, and every promise he makes will turn back on him. The audience knows the myth; the king does not. That gap is dramatic irony.
discussionQuestions: Is a leader responsible for problems he did not knowingly cause? Why or why not?
Where does characterization appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with knowledge and blindness?

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “My children, latest born to Cadmus old, / Why sit ye here as suppliants, in your hands / Branches of olive filleted with wool?” slowly and put it in my own words: The king asks the young people of Thebes, descendants of the city's founder Cadmus, why they sit before him holding olive branches wrapped in wool, the sign of people begging for help. Next, craft. I notice the man famous for answering the Sphinx's riddle opens the play by asking a question, and he speaks to his people as a father to his children. The strongest word is “children”: Oedipus speaks as the father of his city, yet he does not know who his own father is. Then, effect. Why does Oedipus call the suppliants his children? My answer: Oedipus calls the suppliants his children because he sees himself as the protecting father of Thebes; the audience, who knows the myth, hears the irony that this father has never known his own parents.
